ideas.why: The issue says: "The owner's first run hit the token on Create. Done in answer: a vault is created on the device with no token, takes files there, and is sent to the server from..."
ideas.summary: 14 November 2026
detail: 14 November 2026

The owner's first run hit the token on Create. Done in answer: a vault is created on the device with no token, takes files there, and is sent to the server from Share (VaultShelf.sendToServer, VaultSync.transferWithLargeFiles). After that it lives on the server.

Not done, and why: keeping a shared vault on the device with push and pull, as VoiceDebrief does. Two people adding photographs at the same time would diverge and the engine has no merge; and a pull would fetch every video. Both come before that.

ideas.title: A read-only share that can be taken back
ideas.why: The issue's status: "Status: open. A question for the owner."
ideas.summary: A vault key and a read key cannot be revoked. The web Vault UI's token manager has a read-only token with an expiry and a revoke (ro-word-word-1234, a small encrypted record held as a transfer on the server), marked there as a test harness. sgit has no equivalent. Agree one format for the app, sgit and the web UI before building it in the app.
detail: A vault key and a read key cannot be revoked. The web Vault UI's token manager has a read-only token with an expiry and a revoke (ro-word-word-1234, a small encrypted record held as a transfer on the server), marked there as a test harness. sgit has no equivalent. Agree one format for the app, sgit and the web UI before building it in the app.
The web Vault's read-only token, as its source has it (read 14 November 2026)

From the Send repository at da293d4, en-gb/vault/token/vault-token-manager.js and lib/sg-vault/sg-vault-crypto.js. Enough to build it natively; the open question is still whether this is the format to keep.

- The token is adjective-noun-NNNN; ro- is only a prefix in links. - Its record lives on the server as a transfer whose id is the first 12 hex of sha256("ro-token-transfer-v1:" + token). - The record is iv(12) + AES-256-GCM of {"vault_id", "read_key" (base64 of the 32 bytes), "ref_file_id"}, under PBKDF2-SHA256(token, salt sgraph-ro-token-v1, 100,000 rounds). - Create: POST /api/transfers/create with the access key and {file_size_bytes: 0, transfer_id, delete_auth_hash, max_downloads, auto_delete: false, expires_at}, then upload the ciphertext, then POST /api/transfers/complete/{id}. - Open: GET /api/transfers/download/{id}, no access key, then decrypt; the vault is read from bare/refs/<ref_file_id> with the read key. - Revoke: DELETE /api/transfers/delete/{id} with the header x-sgraph-transfer-delete-auth holding the preimage of delete_auth_hash. - The owner's list is a file in the...

ideas.title: "Send to vault" from Photos and Files (a share extension)
ideas.why: Open, with nothing built yet: "Status: open. The plan, written before any code. Owner of the code: the sgit app session."
ideas.summary: What it is
detail: What it is
In Photos, Files or any app's share sheet, an entry "sgit": choose a vault and a folder, and the items go in. It is the shortest road from a camera roll to a team's vault.
How it has to work
A share extension is a separate small program with little memory (about 120 MB) and a short life. It cannot encrypt a video and upload it. So:

1. The extension only takes the files in. It copies each item, file to file, into a folder that the extension and the app both own (an App Group container), with a small record: which vault, which folder, the names. Then it closes. This is the same "copy it in before anything else" rule the outbox already follows. 2. The app does the rest. When the app is next opened it finds those records and turns each into an outbox job, exactly as if the files had been picked in the app. The extension says so plainly: "Kept. Open sgit to send them." 3. The extension never holds a key. It is given only the names and ids of the vaults, which the app writes into the shared folder. Vault keys and the access key stay in the app's Keychain.

What it will not do at first: upload without the app being opened. That needs background uploads (the next item in issue 103), which fits on top of this: the staged ciphertext handed to a background transfer.
What it changes outside the code

- A second target in Apps/SGit/SGit.xcodeproj (the sgit app's own project file), bundle id ai.sgit.vaults.app.share. - An App Group, group.ai.sgit.vaults.app, in the entitlements of the app and of the extension. The outbox's intake folder moves into it. - Signing. Today the release script signs one app with one entitlements file. With an extension it must sign the extension first, with its own entitlements, then the app. scripts/release/testflight.sh is shared with VoiceDebrief, so the sgit app gets its own copy.
ideas.statusLine: Status: open. The plan, written before any code. Owner of the code: the sgit app session.

ideas.title: A gallery of vaults, opened in a browser inside the app
ideas.why: The issue says: "Built: a Gallery screen reached from the list of vaults. Entries have a name, a line about them, a topic and a link; they are grouped by topic and can be..."
ideas.summary: Built: a Gallery screen reached from the list of vaults. Entries have a name, a line about them, a topic and a link; they are grouped by topic and can be searched. An entry opens in the web Vault in the system's browser inside the app. An entry that carries a key this app can open has "Add to my vaults".
detail: Built: a Gallery screen reached from the list of vaults. Entries have a name, a line about them, a topic and a link; they are grouped by topic and can be searched. An entry opens in the web Vault in the system's browser inside the app. An entry that carries a key this app can open has "Add to my vaults".
The list is data, never code, because a link may carry a key and no key is committed:

- entries added on the device, by pasting or scanning a link, kept in the Keychain; - a file showcase.json at the top of any vault on the device: {"v": 1, "entries": [{"name", "description", "topic", "link"}]}.
The gallery ships empty and says how to fill it.
Needed from the owner
One of:

1. A showcase vault (preferred): a vault with showcase.json at its top, and its key added to the app on each device that should show the gallery. Changing the file changes every device's gallery. 2. The links themselves, to be pasted into the app.

For each vault to be shown: a name, one line, a topic, and a link that opens it in the web Vault. For anything shown to outside testers the link should be read-only: a read-only token from the web Vault's token manager (ro-word-word-1234, which can be revoked) or a read key. A vault key lets whoever sees it change the vault.

ideas.title: sgit app: a teammate sent a vault key cannot add to it
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.45.
ideas.summary: Finding 1. Screens settings, add. Found by the teammate and the family organiser, and checked in the code.
detail: Finding 1. Screens settings, add. Found by the teammate and the family organiser, and checked in the code.

A colleague sends a vault key. With it the app opens the vault and reads it. Adding a photo to a vault that lives on the server also needs an access key, and without one the write fails ("writing to it needs an access key. Add one in Settings"). Nothing on the add sheet says so, the person was sent one string, and no screen says where an access key comes from. The app's first job, in the owner's words an easy way for the team to share photos and large videos, stops at the first photo for everyone but the person who made the vault.

To decide, with the owner: how a teammate comes by the right to write. Either the access key travels with the invitation (and the share sheet says so), or the person who shares gives each teammate one, or the server learns to accept a write from anybody who holds a vault's write key. Until then, say it at the moment it matters: on the add sheet when the key is a vault key, and where the plus is tapped, with what to ask the sender for.

ideas.title: sgit app: say whether a file has arrived
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.44.
ideas.summary: Finding 2. Screens vault, vault.folder, vault.list. Found by the teammate, who could not finish "be sure they arrived".
detail: Finding 2. Screens vault, vault.folder, vault.list. Found by the teammate, who could not finish "be sure they arrived".

No screen says whether what is shown is the latest, or whether something just added has reached the server. The design says a file is never shown as in the vault before its commit is pushed and read back; the pictures show only a vault at rest, so a person cannot see the difference between "added" and "arrived".

To do: a line on the vault that says where it stands ("everything here is on the server, checked a minute ago"; "3 of 21 on their way; keep the app open"), a mark on a file that is still on its way, and a plain end ("21 files added and on the server"). "Refresh" is behind the three dots; pulling down should do it.

Done (14 November 2026, green in CI and in the pictures of that run): a line at the top of every folder of a vault says where it stands: on the server and when that was last checked, on this device only, how many files are on their way in ("keep the app open"), or that some did not go in and are kept. Pulling down refreshes.

Left: a mark on a single file that is still on its way (a file is not listed at all until its commit is pushed and read back; the upload card names it); a plain last line when a batch ends ("21 files added and on the server"); a picture of a vault that is not at rest (issue 116).

ideas.title: sgit app: who added it
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.44.
ideas.summary: Finding 3. Screens history, commit. Found by the editor and the teammate.
detail: Finding 3. Screens history, commit. Found by the editor and the teammate.

History and a commit say when and what. Who is a key id, a fingerprint and "This device's key" or not; the commit screen says itself that nothing in the vault ties a key to a name. For a team's photos, "who took these" is the first question.

To do: let a device name itself once (a name kept with its public key in the vault, as VoiceDebrief's Identity does for a device), show that name in History and beside a file, and say "this device" in words. Group History by day.

Done (14 November 2026, green in CI on f2c3b94 and seen in its picture): History is grouped by day, and each commit says "This device" or "Another device (key ...)" in place of a hash; the hash stays on the commit's own screen.

Left, and it needs a decision first: a name for a device. A name has to live in the vault to be seen by the others, which is a change to what a vault holds, read by the sgit command and the web Vault UI as well as this app. Proposed: one small file per device beside its public key (the key id, a name the person chose, signed by that key), written the first time the device adds to a vault, so that a name cannot be claimed for somebody else's key. To agree with the owner and the sgit side before anything is written; until then a commit can only be told apart as this device or another.

ideas.title: sgit app: sharing, for someone who was never told what a key is
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.44.
ideas.summary: Findings 4, 5 and 6. Screens share, vault, settings. Found by the family organiser (it decided them against the app) and the editor.
detail: Findings 4, 5 and 6. Screens share, vault, settings. Found by the family organiser (it decided them against the app) and the editor.

The share sheet says, honestly, what a key allows and that it cannot be taken back. It does not say what the person who receives it does: which app, which button. The way to the sheet is behind three dots. The sheet has a link that opens the vault in a browser, a copy button and a QR code, but a person sees a warning and "Show the vault key" first. Any holder of the vault key can delete everything and cannot be removed; nothing says what happens to a vault if the phone is lost.

To do: a visible "Share" on the vault; the sheet to open with the action ("Send the way in"), the message it sends to carry the steps for the receiver, and the warning beneath; a sentence on a lost phone (the key is on this device only: write it down, or it is gone) where a vault is made and on the share sheet. To decide with the owner: an invitation that may add and may not delete, beside issue 104.

Done (14 November 2026, green in CI and in the pictures of that run): Share is on the vault's toolbar. The sheet opens with "Send the way in", which sends a message with the steps for the receiver, the key and a link for a browser; the warning is beneath it. The Create sheet says the key is kept on this device only and what losing the device means. The add sheet says an access key is also needed to add files (issue 110).
Left: the sentence on a lost phone on the share sheet; the invitation that may add and may not delete, which waits for the owner's decision on issues 104 and 110.

ideas.title: sgit app: getting a folder out, at full quality
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.44.
ideas.summary: Findings 7 and 8. Screens vault.folder, file, share. Found by the editor, whose task it was.
detail: Findings 7 and 8. Screens vault.folder, file, share. Found by the editor, whose task it was.

A file leaves one at a time, by Share or by Save to Photos, and nothing says either hands over the original (Photos may re-encode a video). There is no way to take a folder. The route that gives everything, the sgit command on a computer, is named on the share sheet with no command to copy and no address. A read key does not open in the web Vault UI, so somebody on a laptop who should only look needs this app or the command line.

To do: select several, or "Save this folder to Files", with the size and a count; say "the original, as it was added" where that is true; on the share sheet, the exact line to paste on a computer; for the Mac, the app itself is the answer once it runs there (the design says iPhone, iPad and Mac).

Compiles and its tests pass (14 November 2026, 50c8629); done when somebody has saved a folder on a device: the three dots on any folder offer "Save these N files to Files" with the size; the app fetches each, lays them out as in the vault and hands the folder to the Files app. The file screen says Open and Share hand over the original, byte for byte. Beside the shown vault key, the line to paste on a computer (pip install sgit-ai && sgit clone), with a button that copies it with the key in it.
Left: selecting several files that are not one folder; a read key in the web Vault UI (not this app's to fix); the Mac.

ideas.title: sgit app: the Create sheet, the four keys, and smaller things
ideas.why: Open, and named by the release notes of v0.1.44.
ideas.summary: Findings 9 to 14. Screens create, vaults, add, settings, vault, file, history, commit.
detail: Findings 9 to 14. Screens create, vaults, add, settings, vault, file, history, commit.

- Create. The first screen says a vault you create "needs no account, no access key and no network"; the Create sheet shows a server switch that is on and an access key. Say on the sheet what the switch costs, and let its default be off for a person with no access key. "A new vault is a random key, an empty folder and one signed commit" should not be the first sentence. "Name, for this device only" left two users unsure what name others see: say that others name it themselves. - Four keys: vault key, read key, access key, this device's signing key. "Add a vault by its key" does not say which; the add field offers three kinds at once. One line each, where each first appears, and a different word for the access key, which is not a key to a vault. - A vault's row is an id, an access level and a server's name in typewriter text. "Shared, you can add" or "Only on this phone" says what a...

Done (14 November 2026, green in CI and in the pictures of that run): the Create sheet's switch is off for a person with no access key and the sheet says what turning it on needs; the name is said to be for this device, others name the vault themselves; a vault's row is in words ("Shared: you can add and change", "Only on this device").

Left: one line for each of the four keys where it first appears and another word for the access key; words on the plus and the three dots (Share is out of the dots, History is not); "Remove the access key"; the conversion switch; iPad widths; the small things.

Done after that (14 November 2026, green on 86f0150, seen in the pictures): "Add a vault you were sent" in place of "by its key"; Settings says what the access key is (a pass from whoever runs the server, which opens no vault) and what removing it does; the conversion switch is "Make photos and videos open in any browser".

ideas.title: sgit app: a record of every action, on every device
ideas.why: Open, with nothing built yet: "Status: open. Owner: the sgit app session (session_018yvwtQVQdrYtgUXUXD9cVB)."
ideas.summary: The owner, 14 November 2026: "add a full-blown observability here so you capture every single action that happens on this app across my three devices" (a laptop, an iPad and an iPhone), reusing what VoiceDebrief has.
detail: The owner, 14 November 2026: "add a full-blown observability here so you capture every single action that happens on this app across my three devices" (a laptop, an iPad and an iPhone), reusing what VoiceDebrief has.

Compiles and its tests pass (14 November 2026, a4d6620); done when a report from a device has been read: VoiceDebrief's UsageLog, lane and lane encryption copied into the app; every screen is timed and about thirty actions are recorded; Settings, Your activity shows them and sends the report over the developer's lane as sgit/usage/v1, with the device model and a random install id so that three devices can be told apart. The developer reads it with tools/conductor/conductor.py drain.
Left:

- Nobody has sent a report from a device, and the reader has not been run on one. - Sending is by a button, on each device. To decide with the owner: a switch that sends on its own when the app opens (off by default), so that he does not have to remember on three devices. - What an action carried (how many files, how large, how long an upload took, which error) is not recorded, only that it happened. The vault engine's own log (VaultTrafficLog, Settings, Every step) has the requests and timings and is not in the report. - One copy of the lane code, in the shared package SGitPeople, when that lands; this app's copy then goes. - A picture of the screen.

ideas.title: sgit app: the web Vault inside the app, and its features natively
ideas.why: Open, with nothing built yet: "Status: open. Owner: the sgit app session (session_018yvwtQVQdrYtgUXUXD9cVB)."
ideas.summary: The owner, 14 November 2026: recreate as much as possible of the web Vault's core here (navigate folders, open a file, edit a file, see the HTML preview), and "allow me to open the full web interface here", loading the vault by JavaScript as sgit.ai's embedding does, not by putting the key in the address.
detail: The owner, 14 November 2026: recreate as much as possible of the web Vault's core here (navigate folders, open a file, edit a file, see the HTML preview), and "allow me to open the full web interface here", loading the vault by JavaScript as sgit.ai's embedding does, not by putting the key in the address.

Compiles and its tests pass (14 November 2026, a4d6620); done when it has been used on a device: UI/WebVaultView.swift. The protocol it uses was tried against the live page first, in Chromium, with a throwaway vault: see the reality file's row.
What the try showed, to keep:

- https://dev.vault.sgraph.ai/en-gb/vault/?embed=1, loaded as the page itself (no frame), posts {sg: 'vault-embed-ready'} to its own window; a posted {sg: 'vault-open', key, mode: 'vault', deepLink} opens the vault; it answers {sg: 'vault-ready', vaultName, fileCount}. A file's path as deepLink opens on that file. - The key is not stored by the page. sg-vault-recent is written to local storage; the app's web view keeps no storage after it closes. - An event vault-settings-access-key on <vault-shell> with the access key turns the page writable. This is the page's own internal event, not a documented interface: it may change. - vault.sgraph.ai (production) answered nothing. The app uses the dev host.
Left:

- Nobody has run it on a device. First things to look at: the page's layout on a phone, downloads ("Save"), and whether its HTML preview works in a web view. - With changes allowed, the web Vault's commits are unsigned and it pushes without checking that nobody else pushed first; it also rewrites a folder without the large mark. So: off by default, a warning, and not offered where a vault has large files. The proper fix is in the web Vault. - The vault's name is "Untitled Vault" there: the app's name for a vault is local. - Natively: a simple edit of a text file, and an HTML preview (a sandboxed web view fed from the vault). Not started; the web Vault inside the app covers both meanwhile. - A picture: the screen needs the network, which the picture harness does not have.

ideas.title: People, messages and secrets (the SGitPeople package)
ideas.why: Open, and the reality file lists for it: The people layer, SGitPeople.
ideas.summary: From: the owner, 14 November 2026 (the brief in the article). Session: the people session, branch work/people.
detail: From: the owner, 14 November 2026 (the brief in the article). Session: the people session, branch work/people.

Every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging signed cards; everything they send each other, secrets included, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox. One Swift package, Packages/SGitPeople, used by both apps.
Done in the package (first slice)

ideas.title: A harness inside the app
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.
detail: A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. It draws on SHarness, the owner's design for running agents as small, single-purpose processes that reach the world only through separate, policed doors.

SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.

An app with a model in it has the same problem at a smaller scale. When the model is asked what to do next, something decides whether it may read a file, open a vault, use a key or reach the network. Today that something is scattered through the code. The brief is to make it explicit, in the same shape:

| Door | What passes through it in the app | |---|---| | Network | Every request, to which host, and why | | File system | Reads and writes, as a virtual file system over notes and vaults | | Vault | Opening a vault, reading a path, writing a commit | | Keys | Deriving, signing, encrypting, decrypting: the key never leaves this door | | Model | Every prompt and every answer, on the device or in Apple's cloud | | Run | Whatever the app can execute on the model's behalf, if anything |
Each door is a small component with one job, a policy for what it will do, and a record of what it did. This need not be separate processes on iOS; the shape and the records are what matter first.

The reason to build it this way is to be able to watch it. On an iPad or a Mac: the thing being done on the left, the doors on the right, and each request drawn as it passes from one to the other, allowed or refused. The vault engine's "Every step" log is the first, text-only version of this for one door.
As the interface becomes something the model helps decide (see Two decision engines), this view is how anyone, the developer first, understands why the app did what it did.

ideas.title: A private voice note, and what it would take to use it in a clinic
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model on the device turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works offline. What the person chooses to keep is encrypted on the device into a vault that only their key opens....
detail: Kind: an idea, with corrections. From: a conversation recorded in the app on 13 November 2026 between the owner and a clinician, who asked for it to be written down and drawn. Written up by the agent working on the repository, which has also corrected the places where the conversation described the plan as if it were built, or said more than is true.

VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model on the device turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works offline. What the person chooses to keep is encrypted on the device into a vault that only their key opens. What they choose to send goes to one other person, encrypted to that person's public key, so that the server carrying it holds bytes it cannot read. There is no account with the company that made the app. The proposal is to try this between a patient and a clinician.

| Step | What happens | Today | |---|---|---| | 1. Speak | The recording is written into the app's own storage as it is spoken | Works | | 2. Words | Apple's speech model, on the device, produces a transcript with times | Works. English tried; other languages untried | | 3. Summary | Apple's language model, on the device, writes key points, actions and one sentence | Works, with faults: see below | | 4. Keep | The note is encrypted on the device into a vault as one signed commit | Works by hand; automatic saving is written, untried | | 5. Exchange keys | The clinician shows a QR code: their public key and the address of their inbox. The patient scans it once | In build 0.1.9, untried on a device. The receiving side exists as a script, not an app | | 6. Send | The note is encrypted on the patient's device to the clinician's key and left in their inbox | Works: every note in this project's...

- The models run on the device, so it works offline and the audio need not go anywhere. True of both Apple's speech model and its language model as the app uses them. - No login with us. The app is installed with an Apple ID, which the developer does not see. The developer cannot tell one user from another, and is not meant to. - A passkey is unlocked by a face or a finger and kept by Apple so that only your own devices can use it. True: passkeys live in iCloud Keychain, which is end-to-end encrypted. - A vault's key can be taken out and the vault opened in a browser. True: the vault format is sgit's, and a vault made by the app has been read back that way. - The clinician's side is the same design in a different app. That is the intention: the keys, vaults and inboxes do not change; the screens do.

1. "The model transcribes and separates the speakers." It transcribes. It does not tell speakers apart: the recording this article came from, with two people talking, came out as one unbroken voice. The app treats every note as one person's memo. 2. "The passkey is the same one I use for iCloud." No. A passkey belongs to one site or app. The one used here would be made for this purpose and is separate from the Apple ID. What is shared is where it is kept (iCloud Keychain) and how it is unlocked (Face ID or Touch ID). 3. "The vault key is made from the passkey." That is the design, and it already works on the web at pki.sgit.ai. In the app, the arithmetic exists and is tested against published examples, but the sign-in itself is not built. Today the app keeps vault keys in the device's Keychain. 4. "Because it is on the device and encrypted, it is GDPR compliant." This is the one to be...

Doing the work on the device and encrypting before anything leaves it removes a large part of the usual risk: there is no company server holding recordings, no third-party model receiving them, and a breach of the storage server yields ciphertext. Those are real advantages and they are the reason for the design.
They do not make a service "compliant" by themselves. If a clinic used this with patients:

ideas.why: An article; work it names has begun: issue 110.
ideas.summary: The idea in one line: every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox. VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.
detail: Kind: an architecture and a brief. From: the owner, 14 November 2026: "anybody who installs the app has a public and private key straight away ... register people, kind of like PKI ... identities from the website, and identities shared by QR code, in person or in a WhatsApp message ... a messaging system ... your device becomes the management layer ... a full-blown secrets manager." Written up by the agent working on the repository. Intention, not fact: what is built says what exists.

The idea in one line: every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox. VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.

- Your key pair (RSA-OAEP 4096 to receive, ECDSA P-256 to sign; the sgit key bundle). Made at first launch, kept in iCloud Keychain so that your other devices have it. Built in VoiceDebrief (PKIKit, the Identity screen); made when asked for, not at first launch; untried on a device. - This device's key, in the Secure Enclave where there is one, vouched for by your key. Built in VoiceDebrief; untried. - An inbox: an append lane on a vault of yours. Anyone holding its link can drop a sealed message in; only your key opens it. The lane works today (every note sent to the developer goes this way); an inbox per person is not built. - A contact card: your name, your public keys, your inbox's link, signed by you. Shown as a QR code or a link. Not built: today's QR code carries an inbox link and one public key, not a signed card. - The secrets store: access keys, vault keys, passwords and...

| Way | How | How far to trust it | |---|---|---| | In person | Each scans the other's QR code | The most: you saw the person and the code together | | By a message | The card as a QR picture or a link, on WhatsApp, Signal, email | As far as the channel it came by | | From the register | Look up a name or fingerprint at pki.sgit.ai | As far as the register's checks on that person |

A contact keeps how it was met, and can be checked later (fingerprints compared face to face, or the register vouching). Adding is two-way: when you add someone, the app offers to send them your card, so they can write back. Agents are contacts like any other: a Claude session has a card and an inbox (tools/conductor/ makes them).

A message is sealed to the recipient's public key and signed with the sender's, on the sender's device (the envelope PKIKit already makes). It can carry text, a voice note (what VoiceDebrief sends today), a secret, a vault invitation, or a card.

Checking for new messages. There are no push events, so the app asks: when it opens or comes to the front, every minute while it is in use, and less and less often when idle (the owner's pattern from the website). One list call on one inbox per check: little traffic.

ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap took them.
detail: A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap took them.

Invented users, each with a purpose and a level of knowledge, who walk the screens and report where they hesitated, guessed wrong or got lost. The newsroom at sgit.ai does this for a website, one screenshot at a time. The same applies here.
For example:

- someone who wants to record a memo while driving and has never heard of a vault; - someone careful about privacy who wants to know exactly what leaves the phone; - a developer who wants to see every request the app makes; - someone who lost a recording in another app and does not trust this one.

1. Pictures of every screen. A workflow in continuous integration runs the app in a simulator, one launch per screen with sample data, and keeps a screenshot of each on an iPhone and an iPad. The sibling repository has this already; it is to be carried over. It also gives the agent its first sight of its own work. 2. A walk. A synthetic user is given a task and the screenshots, and says at each step what it would tap and what it expects. Where its expectation and the next screen disagree is a finding. 3. A record. Findings are kept as files, each with the screen, the user and what went wrong, and a status as review findings have elsewhere in this family.

A synthetic user reads a picture. It does not feel a button that is too small for a thumb, hear nothing, or drive a car. Simulators have no speech model and no Apple Intelligence, so screens that depend on them are shown with sample data. The owner on a device remains the test that counts.
ideas.source: A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

detail: A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. Nothing here is built unless what is built says so.

VoiceDebrief for iOS started as one job: a voice note in, a transcript and a debrief out. In a day it gained on-device speech, an on-device model, vaults, signed commits and encrypted lanes, and it runs as one app on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, delivered by TestFlight. That combination is rarer than the product it was built for.

So for now the app is also a laboratory. The product that ships will be smaller and more focused. The lab exists to get the primitives and the key workflows right, and to find out what is possible, before deciding what that product is.
Because nothing here is being submitted to the App Store yet, the lab can ask for any capability Apple offers.

| | Experiment | Question | |---|---|---| | L01 | One prompt, tools on and off | What does the on-device model do with a single tightly scoped prompt and a chosen set of tools? How reliable are its tool calls? | | L02 | The model drives the screen | Can the model choose what the interface shows next, through function calls, from a state the code hands it? | | L03 | The model edits a page | Can it write or change an HTML or JSON page in a vault that the app then renders? | | L04 | Apple's larger model | The same prompts on Private Cloud Compute: what does 32,768 tokens and reasoning buy? | | L05 | Another provider through the same framework | iOS 27 lets a session run on other models, Claude among them. What changes, and what does it cost in privacy? | | L06 | Images | What can Image Playground and image input do for a note: a cover, a photographed whiteboard? | | L07 | A file system for...
Each experiment is a screen in a Lab section of the app, with what was asked, what came back, how long it took and what it cost shown plainly. An experiment that fails is a result.

- An experiment says what it is. Nothing in the lab is presented as a finished feature. - Everything the model is given and everything it returns can be seen. See Two decision engines. - What works is rebuilt properly, and probably moved out into its own app or package. The lab is where it is found, not where it lives.

ideas.title: The vault is a version-controlled store
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could be kept this way and gain history, integrity and a way to move.
detail: A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could be kept this way and gain history, integrity and a way to move.
And a vault is a good way to move data. Two devices, two people or a person and an agent can exchange work by exchanging vaults, or by writing to each other's lanes.

The first vault screen in this app asks for an SG/Send access token before it will create a vault. That is wrong in principle. Creating a vault needs no server and no token. A vault can exist on the device alone. A token is needed only to push it to a server, and the server itself should be something you configure, not something assumed.
So:

- A vault is local first. Create, commit, read and browse with no network. - A server is a remote. Add one, with its address and its token, when you want the vault elsewhere. Push and pull are explicit. - Some things need a remote. A lane, where others write to you, lives on a server. That is one use, not the definition.

| | What | |---|---| | Local vaults | Create and use a vault on the device with no token. The engine already writes to a folder in its tests; the app should use that | | Remotes | A list of servers, each with an address and a token in the Keychain. A vault may have none, one or several | | Several vaults, several lanes | Register them with names. Choose where a note goes: one vault, several, a lane to a person or to an agent that conducts other agents | | A file system | The vault as a virtual file system the app, and later the model, can be given in part: this folder, read only | | Vault apps | A vault can hold an app: pages and data rendered from the vault. Render them here. Then create and edit them here, and see whether the model can | | Graphs | Every note processed into the store, then linked: semantic graphs across notes and across vaults |
ideas.source: A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

ideas.title: Two decision engines
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.
detail: A position. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.
The code owns the states. The model is asked one question at a time.

The application is a set of states and the moves between them: a state machine, as the pipeline already is. At a given state the code may hand the model a small, exact package (this state, this data, these tools) and ask one of two things:

- What should happen next? The model answers by calling a function the code offered. - Say this another way. The model turns one form into another: a transcript into a debrief, a debrief into a title, a request into a query. A translation or a projection, not a conversation.

There is no long history. Each prompt stands alone, built for that state, as small as it can be. That is what makes it cheap enough for an on-device model with a few thousand tokens of context, and it is what makes it inspectable: for any decision the model made, the whole of what it was shown fits on one screen.

- Control. The model can only do what the functions offered at that state allow. A tool that is not offered does not exist for it. - Debugging. A one-prompt decision can be replayed. A decision buried in a long conversation cannot. - Size. Small models are good at small, literal tasks and poor at long ones. This asks them only for the first kind. - Privacy. What leaves the code for the model is chosen each time, and can be shown each time.
ideas.source: A position. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

ideas.title: Voice everywhere
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.
detail: An idea. From the owner's voice memos of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.

Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.

This is why the screen shows the words and the level as you speak. It is not decoration. It is the evidence that the recording is being heard and kept, and it is what lets someone trust the app enough to stop checking it.
It is also why the note exists before the first word and why the recording is kept in a form that survives the app dying. See the design, where capture without loss is the first job.

Recording should not be a place you go to. It should be available from wherever you are: one control, on every screen, that starts a voice memo and returns you to what you were doing. The memo then goes where it should: the library, a vault, a lane to someone else.
The workflow that matters most: speaking while driving or walking, hands and eyes elsewhere, and trusting that it was captured; then, later, giving that memo to a particular person or agent.

There is no reason to pick one interface before trying several. One of them might look less like a recorder and more like an assistant that is listening: a single visual that shows it hears you, in the manner of the assistants in films. The lab is where these are compared, on the phone, the tablet and the laptop.

ideas.title: Where each key lives
ideas.why: An article: a position or a brief. Nothing in it is built unless the reality file says so.
ideas.summary: A passkey, behind Face ID, proves it is you. iCloud Keychain carries your secrets to your other devices, encrypted so that Apple cannot read them. Vaults hold the data, encrypted and version controlled, on a store that sees only ciphertext. Put together: sign in to the same Apple account on a new device, authenticate, the vault keys arrive, the app pulls the vaults, and the same files are there....
detail: A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memos of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. Decided by the owner the same day. None of it is built unless what is built says so.

A passkey, behind Face ID, proves it is you. iCloud Keychain carries your secrets to your other devices, encrypted so that Apple cannot read them. Vaults hold the data, encrypted and version controlled, on a store that sees only ciphertext. Put together: sign in to the same Apple account on a new device, authenticate, the vault keys arrive, the app pulls the vaults, and the same files are there. The vault provides the synchronisation, and when two devices write at once it behaves as git does: the first wins, the second pulls, merges and pushes.

| Key | What it is for | Must it travel? | Where it lives | |---|---|---|---| | Vault keys, server tokens | Open and write vaults | Yes | iCloud Keychain, synchronised. On by default (owner's decision), with a switch to keep them on this device only | | The user's key pair | Who you are: signs as you, lets others encrypt to you | Yes | iCloud Keychain to begin with; the master vault, opened by the passkey, when that is built. Never the Secure Enclave, which cannot let a key out and cannot hold an RSA key | | The device's key pair | Which device, or which install of the app, did this | Never | The Secure Enclave of that device where it can be, otherwise the Keychain marked for this device only. Meant to be lost with the device or the app | | Public halves | Checking the above | Freely | In the vault beside the data. The user's also in a register such as pki.sgit.ai |
Two details that follow:

- A synchronised Keychain item cannot also demand Face ID. That protection exists only for items that stay on one device. It is the main reason the passkey and master vault remain the end state: the passkey is behind Face ID every time, and the keys sit inside a vault rather than loose in the Keychain. - Keychain items survive deleting an app. For the device key to die with the app, the app has to wipe it the first time it runs after a reinstall.

Every commit is already signed by a device key whose public half is in the vault. What is missing is anything that says whose device it is. The addition is a short statement in the vault, signed by the user's key: this device key is mine, from this date, for these uses. A reader then checks two things: the device signed the commit, and the person vouched for the device. Losing a device means withdrawing one statement and nothing else.
The app must work with no register at all. As an option, the owner can connect it to the identity he already has at pki.sgit.ai, where his key pair is kept behind a passkey.

It opens looking only. "Allow changes" hands the page this device's access key for the...
detail: UI/WebVaultView.swift: "Open in the web Vault" on a vault's three dots and on a file. The page dev.vault.sgraph.ai/en-gb/vault/?embed=1 is loaded in a web view that keeps nothing, announces itself, and is handed the vault key by a posted message (the web Vault's embed protocol); the key is not in the address. It opens looking only. "Allow changes" hands the page this device's access key for the visit, after a warning; it is not offered for a vault that holds large files, because the web Vault rewrites a folder without the mark that says a file is large

The protocol was tried on 14 November 2026 against the live page in Chromium with a throwaway vault made by sgit: opened by message, HTML preview shown, a deep link to a file honoured, nothing of the key in the address or in storage, and the access-key event turned "Read-only" into "Synced". The production host vault.sgraph.ai did not answer the handshake. The Swift has unit tests for the words and the host rule; the web view itself has never run on a device or a simulator
